chapters.title: 史前生活、艺术与聚落
chapters.question: 共同体如何组织起来？
chapters.summary: 农业定居带来聚落、墓葬与仪式空间。欧洲各地区的发展并不同步，巨石遗迹提供了文字之前的社会证据。
chapters.next: 从定居社会走向更复杂的城市与政治组织。

chapters.title: 青铜时代的宫殿与城堡
chapters.question: 宫殿如何组织贸易和权力？
chapters.summary: 爱琴海的宫殿、城堡与墓葬记录早期复杂社会。米诺斯与迈锡尼文化有交流，也有不同的政治组织。
chapters.next: 宫殿体系衰落以后，城邦在新的社会条件下逐渐形成。

chapters.title: 城邦与希腊世界
chapters.question: 共享文化，为什么没有一个统一国家？
chapters.summary: 城邦竞争与跨地区圣地同时存在。城邦政治、海上交流与希腊化世界，为后来的地中海历史提供重要背景。
chapters.next: 罗马逐渐把这些互相竞争的地区纳入更大的政治网络。

chapters.title: 罗马共和国与帝国
chapters.question: 辽阔领土靠什么连接？
chapters.summary: 道路、城市、法律与军队把地中海周围连接起来。边疆既是军事界线，也是贸易和人口流动的区域。
chapters.next: 帝国重心与宗教改变；东西部的政治轨迹逐渐分化。

chapters.title: 罗马的转型与延续
chapters.question: 西部帝位消失，罗马就结束了吗？
chapters.summary: 基督教改变公共空间与权力表达。西部出现新的王国，东罗马继续存在；拉文纳留下了多次政权转换的物质证据。
chapters.next: 东罗马延续，西欧则形成新的王权与教会关系。

chapters.title: 加洛林、维京与早期王国
chapters.question: 谁能继承罗马的帝国理想？
chapters.summary: 加洛林统治者与教会共同建构权威。800年查理曼加冕；843年帝国分割。北欧也在王权与基督教化中发生变化。
chapters.next: 欧洲形成多个政治中心，教会、王权与城市彼此竞争。

chapters.title: 教会、王国与商业城市
chapters.question: 权力只属于国王吗？
chapters.summary: 大教堂、大学、商人城市和跨海贸易共同塑造中世纪欧洲。不同区域的王国形成与城市发展并不沿同一节奏。
chapters.next: 城市财富与知识网络为艺术和思想的新变化提供条件。

chapters.title: 伊斯兰、拜占庭与奥斯曼
chapters.question: 欧洲的边界如何成为交流地带？
chapters.summary: 伊比利亚与东地中海同时存在战争、统治转换和文化交流。1453年君士坦丁堡陷落、1492年格拉纳达易手，是两条不同的历史线。
chapters.next: 这些变化与文艺复兴、海上扩张同时发生，不是前后相继的单线。

chapters.title: 文艺复兴与海上扩张
chapters.question: 城市财富如何改变世界观？
chapters.summary: 意大利城市的赞助网络与古典知识重读推动艺术变化；伊比利亚海上扩张连接全球，也带来征服、殖民与剥削。
chapters.next: 新的知识、商业财富和宗教争论冲击既有权威。

chapters.title: 宗教改革与政治分裂
chapters.question: 信仰为什么会重画政治版图？
chapters.summary: 宗教改革涉及信仰、传播与统治权。战争与谈判改变了欧洲秩序；1648年是重要节点，但不是现代国家突然诞生的一年。
chapters.next: 王朝国家继续整合权力，商业共和国发展不同的制度。

chapters.title: 王朝、共和国与启蒙
chapters.question: 谁拥有城市和国家的主导权？
chapters.summary: 宫廷、商人精英与帝国首都呈现不同的权力模式。宫殿和城市规划既展示审美，也组织社会等级和经济活动。
chapters.next: 启蒙思想、财政危机与社会冲突共同通向革命时代。

chapters.title: 革命与民族国家
chapters.question: 臣民如何成为公民？
chapters.summary: 法国革命、拿破仑战争与其后政治重组改变主权观念。民族主义、帝国和自由主义相互竞争，并不只有一种现代化道路。
chapters.next: 工业化加速社会变化，国家动员能力也不断增强。

chapters.title: 工业化与帝国社会
chapters.question: 工厂如何改变日常生活？
chapters.summary: 煤、铁、机器和运输网络改变劳动与城市。工业增长与全球殖民体系相互关联，财富与社会代价必须一起观察。
chapters.next: 大众社会、技术与政治冲突进入20世纪。

chapters.title: 世界大战与现代性危机
chapters.question: 现代社会为何走向大规模毁灭？
chapters.summary: 战争、独裁、种族迫害与大屠杀必须与现代艺术和社会实验并置理解。纪念地的参观以理解受害者和历史责任为中心。
chapters.next: 战后重建、冷战分裂与合作机制同时展开。

chapters.title: 重建、分裂与欧洲合作
chapters.question: 欧洲如何处理共同历史？
chapters.summary: 城市重建、冷战与欧洲一体化塑造战后生活。欧盟是部分欧洲国家的合作制度，不能等同整个欧洲，也不是古代帝国的重现。
chapters.next: 把保存、重建与记忆作为继续理解当代欧洲的入口。

chapters.title: 人类起源与早期技术
chapters.question: 化石与工具如何共同成为历史证据？
chapters.summary: 非洲的人类起源遗址保存化石、工具和环境证据。不同地点的材料要依靠地层和年代研究联系起来，而不能用一件展品讲完人类演化。
chapters.next: 下一章转向岩画、环境与生活方式；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 岩画、环境与生活方式
chapters.date: 史前至历史时期，多地不同步
chapters.question: 图像怎样记录人与环境的关系？
chapters.summary: 岩画、岩刻和聚落遗存呈现狩猎采集、牧养与环境变化。图像的年代和含义需要考古证据与地方知识共同解释。
chapters.next: 下一章转向尼罗河国家与王室建筑；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 尼罗河国家与王室建筑
chapters.question: 国家如何组织庞大的建筑与仪式？
chapters.summary: 尼罗河流域的国家组织将农业资源、劳动力与宗教仪式结合起来。金字塔、神庙与王陵采用不同的空间方式表达王权，不能看作同一时期的建筑。
chapters.next: 下一章转向库施、纳帕塔与麦罗埃；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 库施、纳帕塔与麦罗埃
chapters.question: 尼罗河南部如何形成自己的政治中心？
chapters.summary: 库施是尼罗河南部的重要政治力量。纳帕塔与麦罗埃的王室、宗教和水利遗存呈现本地制度，也记录与埃及等地区的长期交流。
chapters.next: 下一章转向北非与古代地中海；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 北非与古代地中海
chapters.question: 港口与城市如何连接非洲和地中海？
chapters.summary: 腓尼基、布匿、希腊和罗马城市在北非留下不同层次。港口、市场和公共建筑体现非洲并非古代地中海世界的边缘。
chapters.next: 下一章转向红海王国与基督教传统；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 红海王国与基督教传统
chapters.question: 信仰怎样改变城市、山地和王权？
chapters.summary: 非洲东北部形成自己的王国和基督教传统。阿克苏姆、埃及朝圣城市、西奈修道院与埃塞俄比亚岩凿教堂，展示信仰在不同环境中的建筑表达。
chapters.next: 下一章转向伊斯兰城市与北非王朝；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 伊斯兰城市与北非王朝
chapters.question: 政治、宗教与商业如何共同塑造城市？
chapters.summary: 伊斯兰城市的兴起并非单一过程。王朝赞助、宗教教育、港口防御和商业街区，让北非各城市呈现不同的政治与生活结构。
chapters.next: 下一章转向撒哈拉商路与萨赫勒知识网络；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 撒哈拉商路与萨赫勒知识网络
chapters.question: 商路运送的为何不仅是商品？
chapters.summary: 沙漠并未阻止城市与知识网络形成。绿洲聚落、商队古镇和萨赫勒学术中心相互联系，宗教、财富与土建筑传统共同塑造地方历史。
chapters.next: 下一章转向斯瓦希里城市与印度洋；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 斯瓦希里城市与印度洋
chapters.question: 非洲沿海社会怎样参与海上交流？
chapters.summary: 斯瓦希里城市由非洲沿海社会参与印度洋交流而发展。港口、宗教建筑与家庭空间应一起阅读，避免只从外来商人的视角理解城市。
chapters.next: 下一章转向非洲南部的城市与政治组织；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 非洲南部的城市与政治组织
chapters.question: 王室空间与日常聚落如何相互依存？
chapters.summary: 马蓬古布韦与大津巴布韦呈现非洲南部的政治组织和城市发展。高地、围场与居住区之间的关系，比单看石墙更能说明社会结构。
chapters.next: 下一章转向农业、手工业与活态景观；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 农业、手工业与活态景观
chapters.question: 日常生产怎样成为可阅读的历史？
chapters.summary: 历史也保存在梯田、粮仓、冶铁遗存和集会空间中。活态景观仍会改变，参观时需要区分长期传统、现存建筑与今天的社区生活。
chapters.next: 下一章转向本土王国、宫殿与圣地；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 本土王国、宫殿与圣地
chapters.question: 王权如何通过建筑保存自身的叙事？
chapters.summary: 刚果、达荷美、阿散蒂与马达加斯加的王室中心，展示不同的权力和礼仪制度。宫殿叙事也需要与战争、贸易和普通人的生活一起理解。
chapters.next: 下一章转向海上竞争、奴隶贸易与殖民扩张；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 海上竞争、奴隶贸易与殖民扩张
chapters.question: 交流网络如何同时成为控制与剥削的网络？
chapters.summary: 大西洋与印度洋的海上网络伴随贸易、军事竞争和强迫迁移。堡垒与纪念地需要结合奴役者、被奴役者及不同地方社会的历史理解。
chapters.next: 下一章转向殖民城市与现代建筑；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 殖民城市与现代建筑
chapters.question: 如何同时阅读建筑形式与殖民权力？
chapters.summary: 殖民时期的现代建筑既展示材料与形式创新，也体现权力不平等。阿斯马拉提供观察城市规划、公共设施和居住空间分配的入口。
chapters.next: 下一章转向种族隔离、抵抗与公共记忆；主题可能在时间上重叠，并非全洲统一的发展阶段。

chapters.title: 种族隔离、抵抗与公共记忆
chapters.question: 纪念地如何呈现个人经历与制度责任？
chapters.summary: 监狱、见证与纪念展示使制度性压迫成为可讨论的历史。罗本岛是理解南非抵抗与自由的一处入口，并不能代表全非洲独立运动的全部经验。
chapters.next: 继续结合个人观察，思考今天如何保存与解释这些历史。

chapters.title: 土地知识与早期公共工程
chapters.date: 数千年前起，各地不同步
chapters.question: 公共建筑一定以城市和农业为前提吗？
chapters.summary: 平原上的集体狩猎与密西西比河谷的土方工程，呈现不同的土地利用和协作方式。它们不是通往同一种社会的连续阶段。
chapters.next: 继续观察不同地区如何形成城市和区域网络。

chapters.title: 中美洲城市与玛雅诸中心
chapters.date: 前6世纪—16世纪，分地区观察
chapters.question: 不同城市如何组织政治与宗教生活？
chapters.summary: 特奥蒂瓦坎与玛雅诸城的兴衰并不同步。广场、神庙、宫殿与铭文提供观察城市权力、区域交流和地方传统的入口。
chapters.next: 向北对照普韦布洛与密西西比河谷的聚落。

chapters.title: 普韦布洛聚落与密西西比河谷
chapters.question: 聚落怎样组织资源、仪式与区域联系？
chapters.summary: 西南部的普韦布洛建筑与卡霍基亚的土丘城市属于不同环境与传统。并列观察其空间组织，不能把它们归为一个统一帝国。
chapters.next: 下一阶段关注殖民网络与当地社会的变化。

chapters.title: 殖民港口与传教边疆
chapters.question: 殖民制度如何进入城市与日常生活？
chapters.summary: 加勒比港口连接帝国航运，北部边疆的传教站则组织宗教、生产与定居。建筑中的文化交流与殖民统治、强制转变需要一同理解。
chapters.next: 独立运动改变了政治制度，移民继续重塑社会。

chapters.title: 独立、共和国与移民
chapters.question: 自由的政治理念如何成为公共记忆？
chapters.summary: 费城的独立大厅与纽约的自由女神像提供美国建国和跨大西洋公共象征的两条线索。它们不等于北美各国共同的独立史。
chapters.next: 把公共纪念物与当地博物馆中的不同群体经历对照。

chapters.title: 安第斯早期中心与宗教空间
chapters.question: 城市与宗教中心怎样组织人群？

chapters.next: 继续沿海岸与山地比较后来的政治中心。

chapters.title: 沿海王国与印加道路网络

chapters.next: 征服之后，旧有城市和交通网络经历新的权力安排。

chapters.title: 殖民城市、矿业与大西洋联系

chapters.summary: 殖民经济把安第斯白银、巴西黄金和大西洋港口联系起来。城市财富的建筑表现，需要与原住民和被奴役非洲人的劳动经历一同阅读。
chapters.next: 传教聚落提供另一种观察殖民制度与地方社会的尺度。

chapters.title: 瓜拉尼地区的传教聚落

chapters.next: 进入19世纪后，港口和工业生产形成新的全球联系。

chapters.title: 港口、工业与现代首都
chapters.question: 全球贸易与国家建设如何改变城市？
chapters.summary: 瓦尔帕莱索与弗赖本托斯呈现航运、食品工业和世界市场的联系；巴西利亚则将现代规划用于新的国家首都。三者体现不同的现代化路径。
chapters.next: 把规划意图、生产设施与今天的城市使用对照。

chapters.title: 原住民土地知识与食物生产

chapters.summary: 卡卡杜岩画、布吉必姆水产养殖系统与库克早期农业，呈现不同地区持续发展的知识与技术。原住民文化不是只属于过去的遗迹。
chapters.next: 海岛上的仪式中心连接航海、权力与社会记忆。

chapters.title: 海岛网络与仪式中心
chapters.question: 海洋如何连接社会，而不仅是分隔陆地？
chapters.summary: 南马都尔、塔普塔普阿泰亚、拉帕努伊和罗伊·马塔遗址属于不同岛屿传统。石筑空间、航海联系与口述记忆提供理解太平洋社会的入口。
chapters.next: 欧洲殖民扩张带来新的劳动力制度、港口与权力关系。

chapters.title: 殖民劳役与港口社会
chapters.question: 殖民制度如何塑造聚落与劳动？
chapters.summary: 澳大利亚监狱遗址记录流放与强制劳动；莱武卡呈现太平洋港口的贸易和殖民行政。比较这些遗址时，也要观察当地社会的持续存在。
chapters.next: 20世纪的战争、核试验与公共建筑留下不同的现代遗产。

chapters.title: 核时代与现代公共文化
chapters.question: 技术与国家权力留下了什么公共记忆？
chapters.summary: 比基尼环礁记录冷战核试验及居民迁移；悉尼歌剧院呈现战后公共文化与建筑实验。它们提供不同尺度的20世纪历史入口。
chapters.next: 结合当地社区的叙述，继续理解遗产的当代意义。

chapters.title: Prehistoric life, art and settlements
chapters.question: How did communities organise themselves?
chapters.summary: Before writing, art, settlements, tombs and ceremonial places offer evidence of social life. Farming brought new forms of settlement, but regions developed at different times.
chapters.next: Settled societies developed more complex urban and political organisations.

chapters.title: Bronze Age palaces and citadels
chapters.question: How did palaces organise trade and power?
chapters.summary: Aegean palaces, citadels and tombs record early complex societies. Minoan and Mycenaean cultures exchanged ideas but organised political life differently.
chapters.next: After palatial systems declined, city-states gradually emerged under new social conditions.

chapters.title: City-states and the Greek world
chapters.question: Why did shared culture not create a single state?
chapters.summary: Competing cities coexisted with shared sanctuaries. Civic politics, maritime exchange and the Hellenistic world shaped later Mediterranean history.
chapters.next: Rome gradually integrated these competing regions into a larger political network.

chapters.title: Roman Republic and Empire
chapters.question: What connected a vast territory?
chapters.summary: Roads, cities, law and armies connected the Mediterranean. Frontiers were both military boundaries and places of trade and migration.
chapters.next: Shifts in imperial centres and religion contributed to diverging eastern and western political trajectories.

chapters.title: Rome transformed and continued
chapters.question: Did Rome end when the western imperial office disappeared?
chapters.summary: Christianity transformed public space and expressions of power. New kingdoms emerged in the west while the Eastern Roman Empire continued; Ravenna preserves evidence of successive regimes.
chapters.next: Eastern Rome endured while new relationships between rulers and churches developed in western Europe.

chapters.title: Carolingians, Vikings and early kingdoms
chapters.question: Who could inherit Rome’s imperial ideal?
chapters.summary: Carolingian rulers and churches constructed authority together. Charlemagne was crowned in 800; the empire was divided in 843. Northern societies also changed through kingship and Christianisation.
chapters.next: Multiple political centres developed, with churches, rulers and cities competing for power.

chapters.title: Churches, kingdoms and trading cities
chapters.question: Did power belong only to kings?
chapters.summary: Cathedrals, universities, merchant cities and maritime trade shaped medieval Europe. Kingdoms and cities developed along different regional paths.
chapters.next: Urban wealth and knowledge networks helped create conditions for artistic and intellectual change.

chapters.title: Islamic, Byzantine and Ottoman worlds
chapters.question: How did borders become zones of exchange?
chapters.summary: War, changes of rule and cultural exchange coexisted in Iberia and the eastern Mediterranean. Constantinople in 1453 and Granada in 1492 mark different historical trajectories.
chapters.next: These developments overlapped the Renaissance and maritime expansion rather than forming a single sequence.

chapters.title: Renaissance and maritime expansion
chapters.question: How did urban wealth change views of the world?
chapters.summary: Italian patronage and renewed study of antiquity encouraged artistic change. Iberian maritime expansion connected distant regions while bringing conquest, colonisation and exploitation.
chapters.next: New knowledge, commercial wealth and religious disputes challenged established authority.

chapters.title: Reformation and political division
chapters.question: Why did belief reshape political boundaries?
chapters.summary: The Reformation involved faith, communication and political authority. War and negotiation changed European order; 1648 was important, but modern states did not appear overnight.
chapters.next: Dynastic states continued to consolidate power, while commercial republics developed different institutions.

chapters.title: Dynasties, republics and Enlightenment
chapters.question: Who controlled cities and states?
chapters.summary: Courts, merchant elites and imperial capitals embodied different forms of power. Palaces and urban plans organised social hierarchies and economic activity as well as taste.
chapters.next: Enlightenment ideas, financial crises and social conflict contributed to the age of revolutions.

chapters.title: Revolutions and nation-states
chapters.question: How did subjects become citizens?
chapters.summary: The French Revolution, Napoleonic wars and subsequent settlements changed ideas of sovereignty. Nationalism, empires and liberalism competed; there was no single path to modernity.
chapters.next: Industrialisation accelerated social change and increased states’ capacity to mobilise populations.

chapters.title: Industrialisation and imperial societies
chapters.question: How did factories change everyday life?
chapters.summary: Coal, iron, machinery and transport transformed work and cities. Industrial growth was intertwined with colonial systems; wealth and social costs need to be considered together.
chapters.next: Mass society, technology and political conflict carried into the twentieth century.

chapters.title: World wars and the crisis of modernity
chapters.question: Why did modern societies turn to mass destruction?
chapters.summary: War, dictatorship, persecution and the Holocaust must be considered alongside modern art and social experiments. Memorial visits centre victims’ experiences and historical responsibility.
chapters.next: Reconstruction, Cold War division and institutions of cooperation developed together.

chapters.title: Reconstruction, division and cooperation
chapters.question: How does Europe deal with shared history?
chapters.summary: Rebuilding, the Cold War and European integration shaped postwar life. The EU is a cooperative institution of some European countries, not the whole continent or a reborn ancient empire.
chapters.next: Preservation, reconstruction and memory offer ways to continue exploring contemporary Europe.

chapters.title: Human origins and early technologies
chapters.question: How do fossils and tools become historical evidence?
chapters.summary: African human-origins sites preserve fossils, tools and environmental evidence. Stratigraphy and dating connect finds across places; no single object tells the whole story of evolution.
chapters.next: Next: Rock art, environments and lifeways. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Rock art, environments and lifeways
chapters.date: Prehistory into historical periods; regional chronologies differ
chapters.question: How do images record relationships with environments?
chapters.summary: Rock paintings, engravings and settlements illuminate hunting, gathering, herding and environmental change. Archaeological evidence and local knowledge both inform their interpretation.
chapters.next: Next: Nile states and royal architecture. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Nile states and royal architecture
chapters.question: How did states organise monumental building and ritual?
chapters.summary: Nile states brought agricultural resources, labour and ritual together. Pyramids, temples and royal tombs expressed authority differently and belong to distinct historical settings.
chapters.next: Next: Kush, Napata and Meroe. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Kush, Napata and Meroe
chapters.question: How did the southern Nile develop its own political centres?
chapters.summary: Kush was a major political power on the southern Nile. Napatan and Meroitic royal, religious and water-management remains reveal local institutions and sustained exchange with Egypt and other regions.
chapters.next: Next: North Africa and the ancient Mediterranean. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: North Africa and the ancient Mediterranean
chapters.question: How did ports and cities connect Africa with the Mediterranean?
chapters.summary: Phoenician, Punic, Greek and Roman cities left distinct layers in North Africa. Ports, markets and public buildings reveal Africa’s integral role in the ancient Mediterranean.
chapters.next: Next: Red Sea kingdoms and Christian traditions. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Red Sea kingdoms and Christian traditions
chapters.date: Antiquity to the 13th century and beyond
chapters.question: How did faith reshape cities, mountains and royal authority?
chapters.summary: Northeast Africa developed its own kingdoms and Christian traditions. Aksum, Egyptian pilgrimage centres, Sinai monasticism and Ethiopian rock-cut churches show faith expressed in different environments.
chapters.next: Next: Islamic cities and North African dynasties. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Islamic cities and North African dynasties
chapters.question: How did politics, religion and commerce shape cities together?
chapters.summary: Islamic urban development followed varied paths. Dynastic patronage, religious education, coastal defence and markets produced different political and social structures across North Africa.
chapters.next: Next: Saharan trade and Sahelian knowledge networks. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Saharan trade and Sahelian knowledge networks
chapters.question: Why did trade routes carry more than goods?
chapters.summary: Deserts did not prevent urban and intellectual networks. Oasis settlements, caravan towns and Sahelian scholarly centres connected religion, wealth and earthen-building traditions.
chapters.next: Next: Swahili cities and the Indian Ocean. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Swahili cities and the Indian Ocean
chapters.question: How did African coastal societies participate in maritime exchange?
chapters.summary: Swahili towns developed through African coastal participation in Indian Ocean exchange. Ports, religious buildings and domestic spaces should be read together, beyond the perspective of visiting merchants.
chapters.next: Next: Cities and political organisation in southern Africa. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Cities and political organisation in southern Africa
chapters.question: How did royal and everyday settlements depend on each other?
chapters.summary: Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe reveal political organisation and urban development in southern Africa. Relationships among hills, enclosures and dwellings explain more than walls viewed alone.
chapters.next: Next: Farming, craft and living landscapes. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Farming, craft and living landscapes
chapters.question: How can everyday production become readable history?
chapters.summary: History survives in terraces, granaries, ironworking remains and meeting spaces. Living landscapes continue to change; distinguish long traditions, surviving structures and contemporary community life.
chapters.next: Next: Indigenous kingdoms, palaces and sacred places. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Indigenous kingdoms, palaces and sacred places
chapters.question: How did royal authority preserve its narratives through buildings?
chapters.summary: Royal centres in Kongo, Dahomey, Asante and Madagascar reveal varied political and ritual institutions. Palace narratives need to be read alongside warfare, trade and ordinary lives.
chapters.next: Next: Maritime rivalry, slave trading and colonial expansion. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Maritime rivalry, slave trading and colonial expansion
chapters.question: How did networks of exchange also become systems of control and exploitation?
chapters.summary: Atlantic and Indian Ocean networks involved trade, military rivalry and forced movement. Forts and memorials require attention to enslaved people, enslavers and different local societies.
chapters.next: Next: Colonial cities and modern architecture. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Colonial cities and modern architecture
chapters.question: How can we read architectural form alongside colonial power?
chapters.summary: Colonial modern architecture combined formal and material innovation with unequal power. Asmara provides an entry into planning, public infrastructure and the allocation of residential space.
chapters.next: Next: Apartheid, resistance and public memory. Themes may overlap in time rather than form continent-wide stages.

chapters.title: Apartheid, resistance and public memory
chapters.question: How do memorial sites present individual experience and institutional responsibility?
chapters.summary: Prisons, testimonies and memorial interpretation make institutional oppression legible. Robben Island offers one entry into South African resistance and freedom, not the full experience of African independence movements.
chapters.next: Continue with personal observations on how these histories are preserved and interpreted today.

chapters.title: Land knowledge and early public works
chapters.date: Several millennia ago onwards; regional variation
chapters.question: Do public works always require cities and farming?
chapters.summary: Collective hunting on the plains and earthworks in the Mississippi valley reveal different forms of land use and cooperation, not successive steps towards one social model.
chapters.next: Next, explore the emergence of cities and regional networks.

chapters.title: Mesoamerican cities and Maya centres
chapters.date: 6th century BCE–16th century CE; regional histories
chapters.question: How did different cities organise political and religious life?
chapters.summary: Teotihuacan and Maya cities followed different trajectories. Plazas, temples, palaces and inscriptions offer evidence of urban authority, exchange and local traditions.
chapters.next: Compare these cities with Pueblo settlements and Mississippi valley centres.

chapters.title: Pueblo settlements and the Mississippi valley
chapters.question: How did settlements organise resources, ceremonies and regional ties?
chapters.summary: Pueblo architecture in the Southwest and the mound centre at Cahokia belonged to different environments and traditions. Comparing their spatial organisation does not imply a shared empire.
chapters.next: Next, examine colonial networks and changes in local societies.

chapters.title: Colonial ports and mission frontiers
chapters.question: How did colonial institutions shape cities and daily life?
chapters.summary: Caribbean ports served imperial shipping while frontier missions organised religion, production and settlement. Cultural exchange in these buildings must be read alongside colonial rule and coercion.
chapters.next: Independence changed political institutions while migration continued to reshape society.

chapters.title: Independence, republics and migration
chapters.question: How do political ideals of liberty become public memory?
chapters.summary: Independence Hall and the Statue of Liberty provide two US-focused threads: state formation and a transatlantic public symbol. They do not stand for every North American independence history.
chapters.next: Compare public monuments with the experiences of different communities in local museums.

chapters.title: Early Andean centres and sacred spaces
chapters.question: How did urban and religious centres organise people?
chapters.summary: Caral’s platform complexes and Chavin’s ceremonial spaces belong to different periods. They reveal complex Andean histories long before the Inca.
chapters.next: Compare later political centres along the coast and in the highlands.

chapters.title: Coastal kingdoms and Inca road networks
chapters.question: How did terrain and roads shape political integration?
chapters.summary: Chan Chan reveals Chimu urban organisation; Cuzco, Machu Picchu and the Andean road system connect Inca authority with mountain engineering. Inca expansion incorporated earlier societies and infrastructure.
chapters.next: Conquest brought new arrangements of power to existing cities and networks.

chapters.title: Colonial cities, mining and Atlantic connections
chapters.question: How did ports, mines and cities form an economic system?
chapters.summary: Colonial economies connected Andean silver, Brazilian gold and Atlantic ports. Buildings expressing urban wealth should be read alongside Indigenous labour and the experiences of enslaved Africans.
chapters.next: Mission settlements offer another scale for examining colonial institutions and local societies.

chapters.title: Mission settlements in Guarani lands
chapters.question: How did mission institutions reshape settlements and work?
chapters.summary: Jesuit settlements combined churches, plazas, housing and production. Their remains offer a way to discuss Guarani experiences, religious change and colonial order.
chapters.next: In the 19th century, ports and industry formed new global connections.

chapters.title: Ports, industry and a modern capital
chapters.question: How did global trade and state-building change cities?
chapters.summary: Valparaiso and Fray Bentos connect shipping, food production and world markets; Brasilia applies modern planning to a new national capital. They represent different paths of modernisation.
chapters.next: Compare design intentions and industrial facilities with how cities are used today.

chapters.title: Indigenous land knowledge and food production
chapters.date: Deep history to the present; regional chronologies
chapters.question: How have communities managed land and water over time?
chapters.summary: Kakadu rock art, Budj Bim aquaculture and early agriculture at Kuk reveal evolving knowledge and technologies in different regions. Indigenous cultures are living traditions, not simply remains of the past.
chapters.next: Island ceremonial centres connect seafaring, authority and social memory.

chapters.title: Island networks and ceremonial centres
chapters.question: How did the ocean connect societies rather than simply divide land?
chapters.summary: Nan Madol, Taputapuatea, Rapa Nui and Roi Mata’s sites belong to distinct island traditions. Stone-built spaces, maritime connections and oral memory offer ways into Pacific histories.
chapters.next: European colonial expansion introduced new labour systems, ports and power relations.

chapters.title: Colonial labour and port societies
chapters.question: How did colonial institutions shape settlement and labour?
chapters.summary: Australian convict sites record transportation and forced labour; Levuka reveals trade and colonial administration in a Pacific port. Local societies remained active within these changing settings.
chapters.next: War, nuclear testing and public architecture left contrasting modern legacies.

chapters.title: The nuclear age and modern public culture
chapters.question: What public memories have technology and state power left?
chapters.summary: Bikini records Cold War nuclear testing and displacement; Sydney Opera House reveals postwar public culture and architectural experimentation. They offer contrasting entry points into 20th-century history.
chapters.next: Continue with local community accounts to understand these sites’ present significance.

sites.name: Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites
sites.why: Megalithic monuments show how prehistoric communities organised shared labour and ritual.
sites.see: Compare stone arrangements, earthworks and burial landscapes rather than only the isolated stone circle.
sites.question: Why invest so much collective work without modern machinery?

sites.name: Heart of Neolithic Orkney
sites.why: Settlements and ceremonial remains reveal everyday life alongside beliefs.
sites.see: Compare the houses at Skara Brae with the Ring of Brodgar.
sites.question: How were homes, tombs and ceremonial places connected?

sites.name: Acropolis, Athens
sites.why: Athens expressed wealth, religion and civic identity on the Acropolis.
sites.see: Look at the Parthenon, Propylaea and changes in elevation; distinguish restoration from original fabric.
sites.question: How does public architecture express a city's view of itself?

sites.name: Archaeological Site of Delphi
sites.why: A sanctuary shared by rival cities shows that political division could coexist with shared culture.
sites.see: Follow the Sacred Way past city treasuries and the Temple of Apollo.
sites.question: Why display rival cities' wealth in a common sanctuary?

sites.name: Historic Centre of Rome
sites.period: Ancient Rome to the modern era
sites.why: Imperial public spaces and later church power overlap in the same city.
sites.see: Compare the Roman Forum, Colosseum and later churches by their individual dates.
sites.question: How did old buildings acquire new uses as power shifted?

sites.name: Frontiers of the Roman Empire
sites.why: This transnational property preserves parts of an imperial frontier system.
sites.see: Choose a section and compare forts, gates and terrain.
sites.question: Did the frontier simply block movement, or regulate it?

sites.name: Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna
sites.why: Western Roman, Ostrogothic and Byzantine rule left traces in one city.
sites.see: Study the Justinian and Theodora mosaics in San Vitale.
sites.question: Why place rulers at the centre of religious imagery?

sites.name: Historic Areas of Istanbul
sites.why: Successive empires reused the capital while changing the functions of its buildings.
sites.see: Compare Hagia Sophia's architectural layers, the land walls and Ottoman buildings.
sites.question: How do conquerors adapt an inherited capital?

sites.name: Aachen Cathedral
sites.why: Charlemagne's palace chapel linked religion, kingship and imperial ambition.
sites.see: Compare the octagonal core and upper gallery with the later Gothic choir.
sites.question: How does architecture make authority visible?

sites.name: Jelling Mounds, Runic Stones and Church
sites.why: A northern comparison for kingship and Christianisation alongside the Carolingian world.
sites.see: Examine the relationship between the runestones, burial mounds and church.
sites.question: How do words, images and religion tell a royal story?
sites.nameEn: Jelling Mounds, Runic Stones and Church

sites.name: Hanseatic City of Lübeck
sites.why: Merchant cities reveal trade networks and political power beyond dynastic courts.
sites.see: Look at the town hall, brick churches and merchants' streets; distinguish surviving fabric from rebuilding.
sites.question: How could commercial wealth support urban autonomy?

sites.name: Historic Centre of Prague
sites.why: Castle, bridge and old town bring royal power and urban life into one landscape.
sites.see: Compare the positions of Prague Castle, St Vitus Cathedral and Charles Bridge.
sites.question: How did rulers, clergy and citizens share and contest the city?

sites.name: Historic Centre of Kraków
sites.why: Royal, commercial and Jewish spaces reveal the city's multiple communities.
sites.see: Explore Wawel Hill, the Main Market Square and Kazimierz.
sites.question: Which communities shaped different parts of the city?

sites.name: Alhambra, Generalife and Albayzín, Granada
sites.why: Nasrid buildings preserve the court culture of Muslim rule in Iberia.
sites.see: Observe courtyards, water channels, inscriptions and the Albayzín, noting their different dates.
sites.question: How do water, writing and geometry express power?

sites.name: Historic Centre of Florence
sites.why: Commercial wealth, civic politics and artistic patronage reinforced one another.
sites.see: Compare the cathedral dome, Piazza della Signoria and Medici buildings.
sites.question: Who paid for art, and who decided its message?

sites.name: Luther Memorials in Eisleben and Wittenberg
sites.why: Buildings associated with Luther connect the Reformation to particular cities.
sites.see: Visit the Castle Church, Town Church and house exhibitions; separate events from later memorial changes.
sites.question: How did a local religious dispute spread across Europe?
sites.nameEn: Luther Memorials in Eisleben and Wittenberg

sites.name: Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg and Related Groups of Monuments
sites.why: An imperial capital's design expressed dynastic power and engagement with European culture.
sites.see: Read the Neva waterfront, squares and palace axes together.
sites.question: Why give a new capital such a deliberate spatial order?
sites.nameEn: Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg and Related Groups of Monuments

sites.name: Historic Centre of Vienna
sites.why: Court spaces and the Ringstrasse allow comparison between imperial power and a modern metropolis.
sites.see: Compare the Hofburg area and public buildings along the Ringstrasse.
sites.question: How did a court capital adapt to civic society and population growth?

sites.name: Budapest, including the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
sites.why: Urban expansion reveals tensions between national identity and Habsburg imperial structures.
sites.see: Compare Buda Castle, the Parliament waterfront and Andrássy Avenue.
sites.question: How can public buildings express both national and imperial identities?
sites.nameEn: Budapest, including the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue

sites.name: Ironbridge Gorge
sites.why: The landscape connects raw materials, energy, manufacturing and transport.
sites.see: Study the Iron Bridge, Coalbrookdale remains and the industrial valley.
sites.question: Why did industry concentrate here?

sites.name: Bauhaus and its Sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau
sites.why: Modern design's social ambitions contrast with the political crises of the same period.
sites.see: Examine the Dessau school's glass façade, functional layout and associated housing.
sites.question: Can design transform ordinary lives?
sites.nameEn: Bauhaus and its Sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau

sites.name: Auschwitz Birkenau
sites.why: A historical site and memorial to Nazi persecution and the Holocaust.
sites.see: Use official interpretation, survivors' testimony and camp remains to understand systematic persecution.
sites.question: How can individual lives help explain institutional violence without treating this as an ordinary attraction?

sites.name: Strasbourg, Grande-Île and Neustadt
sites.why: Architecture records intertwined French and German histories; postwar cooperation is a related topic for further study.
sites.see: Compare the streets, buildings and scale of the Grande-Île and Neustadt.
sites.question: How does a border city accommodate changing national identities?

sites.name: Monastery of the Hieronymites and Tower of Belém in Lisbon
sites.why: Maritime expansion and royal patronage funded monumental building at Belém.
sites.see: Compare monastery decoration, the tower and their relationship to the Tagus.
sites.question: Where did the wealth come from, and who bore its costs?
sites.nameEn: Monastery of the Hieronymites and Tower of Belém in Lisbon

sites.name: Palace and Park of Versailles
sites.why: Court society and the political crisis of 1789 can be studied at the same place.
sites.see: Examine ceremonial rooms, the Hall of Mirrors and garden axes, comparing uses before and after the Revolution.
sites.question: How did ceremony organise elites, and why did royal control fail?

sites.name: Zollverein Coal Mine Industrial Complex in Essen
sites.why: Mining, coal washing and coking facilities reveal an integrated industrial system.
sites.see: Follow coal through the shafts, washing plant and coke works.
sites.question: How did technical systems change working lives and the regional economy?
sites.nameEn: Zollverein Coal Mine Industrial Complex in Essen

sites.name: Rietveld Schröderhuis (Rietveld Schröder House)
sites.why: An experimental house shows modernism reorganising everyday life.
sites.see: Consider movable partitions, connected spaces and colours in relation to residents' needs.
sites.question: How might different spaces change family life?

sites.name: Seventeenth-Century Canal Ring Area of Amsterdam
sites.why: A merchant republic's expansion combines commerce, engineering and social hierarchy.
sites.see: Compare canal plots, merchants' houses and bridges, paying attention to the allocation of space.
sites.question: How did global trade shape the city while concealing colonial relationships?
sites.nameEn: Seventeenth-Century Canal Ring Area of Amsterdam

sites.name: Historic Centre of Warsaw
sites.why: Rebuilding made the city a place of choices about memory and identity.
sites.see: Compare the Old Town Market Square and rebuilding interpretation with historical images.
sites.question: Why can a reconstructed city retain historical value?

sites.name: Le Havre, the City Rebuilt by Auguste Perret
sites.why: Unlike Warsaw, this reconstruction adopted a modern architectural language.
sites.see: Observe concrete modules, street plans and St Joseph's Church.
sites.question: How should rebuilding balance an earlier appearance with new ways of living?
sites.nameEn: Le Havre, the City Rebuilt by Auguste Perret

sites.name: Brú na Bóinne — Archaeological Ensemble of the Bend of the Boyne
sites.why: Passage tombs such as Newgrange reveal ritual and collective engineering.
sites.see: Study mound forms, carved stones and passage alignments with site interpretation.
sites.question: How were celestial events, burial and collective memory connected?
sites.nameEn: Brú na Bóinne — Archaeological Ensemble of the Bend of the Boyne

sites.name: Birka and Hovgården
sites.why: The Viking Age involved long-distance trade and settlement as well as conquest.
sites.see: Compare harbour, settlement, defensive and burial remains with excavated objects.
sites.question: Which networks connected this northern settlement to distant places?

sites.name: Bryggen
sites.why: Harbour warehouses preserve the organisation of Hanseatic commerce.
sites.see: Observe waterfront timber buildings, narrow passages and storage layouts, noting rebuilding after fires.
sites.question: How did the journey from ship to storehouse shape a neighbourhood?

sites.name: Old City of Berne
sites.why: Streets and plots reveal long-term continuity in urban planning.
sites.see: Study the main street, arcades, fountains and river bend.
sites.question: Why did later rebuilding retain the medieval urban framework?

sites.name: La Grand-Place, Brussels
sites.period: Medieval town hall and late-17th-century rebuilding
sites.why: Guild houses and the town hall express corporate wealth and public identity.
sites.see: Compare the emblems, scale and positions of guild façades and municipal buildings.
sites.question: How does a square allow different groups to represent themselves?

sites.name: Historic Centre of Sighişoara
sites.why: A Transylvanian city provides an entry into migration, commerce and defence.
sites.see: Look for evidence of guilds and civic organisation in walls, towers and streets.
sites.question: How did migrant communities establish urban life in a frontier region?

sites.name: Historic Centre (Old Town) of Tallinn
sites.why: Baltic trade and political authority occupied distinct spaces in the upper and lower towns.
sites.see: Compare the hilltop town, lower town, town hall and merchants' houses.
sites.question: How do terrain and social status divide a city?

sites.name: Studenica Monastery
sites.why: An Orthodox monastery connects Serbian dynasties with Byzantine culture.
sites.see: Study stone church exteriors, frescoes and the whole monastic layout.
sites.question: How did a local dynasty express its identity through religious art?

sites.name: Boyana Church
sites.why: Church painting provides evidence of medieval Bulgarian society and religious culture.
sites.see: Look closely at figures, clothing, expressions and the relationship between building phases.
sites.question: What can religious images reveal about their patrons and society?

sites.name: Archaeological Site of Aigai (Vergina)
sites.why: Palace and royal tombs reveal Macedonian kingship.
sites.see: Compare ceremonial palace spaces with the expression of status in burials.
sites.question: What do these remains reveal about power and society?

sites.name: Archaeological Site of Mystras
sites.why: The hillside town preserves late Byzantine political and religious spaces.
sites.see: Follow the castle, palace and churches through the levels of the town.
